conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I've been reviewing why you came in. You've been having abdominal pain, nausea, chest pain, and eye swelling—is that right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s correct. The belly pain and vomiting have gotten worse over the last two weeks. I think it might be from restarting methotrexate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Methotrexate can sometimes cause nausea and stomach upset. We also saw your CT scan—it didn’t show a bowel obstruction or blood clot in your neck, which we were worried about.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, good. I was scared it was my Crohn’s acting up again or another blockage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your Crohn’s doesn’t seem to be flaring—no diarrhea or bleeding. But your abdomen is tender, and you hadn’t passed gas in 24 hours when you arrived, so we’re watching closely for pseudo-obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pseudo-obstruction? What’s that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s when the bowel acts blocked, but there’s no physical obstruction. It can happen after surgeries or with certain medications. We’ll keep you NPO for now and give IV fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And the chest pain? It wakes me up at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ECG was normal, and your troponins are negative, so it’s unlikely to be your heart. It might be from straining when you vomit or gas buildup. We’ll monitor it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eyes were swollen. That’s gone now, but I had a weird noise in my ear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The eye swelling resolved, which is reassuring. The ear thing and the lung changes on your CT are a bit unclear. But your ANCA test was negative, so it’s probably not vasculitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Lung changes? What kind of changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: There are some small nodules and hazy spots in your lungs. They’ve been there before, and a pulmonologist reviewed them—they don’t look like infection or cancer. We’ll follow with X-rays.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. Can I at least get my Dilaudid on schedule? I need it every few hours for the pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ve started your usual IV Dilaudid, Benadryl, and diazepam as needed. We’ll keep it consistent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your belly is more distended today, and you’re still nauseated. We’re going to place an NG tube to help decompress your stomach.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An NG tube? I hate those. It’s so uncomfortable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I know it’s not pleasant, but it will help reduce the pressure and nausea. We’ll make sure it’s placed correctly with an X-ray.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Alright, if it helps. How much fluid came out?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Over 2.5 liters already. That’s a lot, and it confirms your bowel isn’t moving things through properly. But no obstruction on imaging—this supports pseudo-obstruction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not a real blockage?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not a physical one. Your bowel just isn’t contracting well. We’ll keep the NG tube in for a few days and let your gut rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your repeat X-rays show no change—still no obstruction. The NG tube is working. How are you feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still nauseous, but the pain is a bit better. Can I try sipping water?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. We need to make sure your bowel is ready. We’ll wait until your nausea improves and the NG output decreases.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture came back negative, so we’re stopping the Cipro. The initial test showed bacteria, but it wasn’t a true infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I was worried about a UTI.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. Your symptoms are from your gut, not your bladder. We’re also stopping methotrexate for now—it might be contributing to your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Should I restart it later?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Discuss it with your GI doctor. Given your reaction, they might adjust the dose or switch meds.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your NG output has decreased, and you’re less bloated. We’re going to try removing the tube and start clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank goodness. I pulled it out once yesterday, but then I vomited and they put it back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we saw that. This time, we’ll go slow—sips of water, then broth. If you keep it down, we’ll advance your diet.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You tolerated the clear liquids well. Today, we’ll try soft solids—applesauce, toast, maybe some Ensure.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hungry. Can I have more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Let’s not rush. Your gut has been through a lot. We’ll build up slowly to avoid setbacks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—you passed gas and had a small bowel movement. That means your gut is waking up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Finally! I was starting to worry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Me too. We’ll keep advancing your diet. You’re on track to go home soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve been tolerating soft foods well. No vomiting, pain is controlled with oral meds. We’re thinking discharge in a couple of days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about my lung nodules? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The pulmonologist says they’re stable and likely not serious. No signs of infection or cancer. Just follow up with chest X-rays as planned.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my eye swelling and ear noise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The eye swelling resolved on its own. The ear thing doesn’t seem linked to anything serious. If it persists, see ENT as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. You’re on your regular pain meds by mouth, eating soft foods, and your abdomen is soft. We’re planning discharge tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What meds will I go home on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Same as before—Dilaudid, tramadol, oxazepam, Pepogest, Slomag. We’re restarting bupropion too, since you stopped it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And methotrexate?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hold off for now. Talk to your GI doctor before restarting. We’ll send a note to them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re stable, pain is controlled, and you’re tolerating food.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What should I watch for at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: If you develop severe pain, can’t keep food down, run a fever, or stop passing gas, come back right away.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP in a week, GI doctor to discuss methotrexate, and pulmonology for chest X-rays. We’ll send all the records.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final check before discharge. Any new symptoms?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel much better. Still a little tired, but the pain is way down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s expected. Your body’s been through a lot. Keep resting, eat small meals, and take your meds as prescribed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’m glad this is over.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Call if anything changes. We’re here if you need us.
